scoreNote: Strong (5): grants that media coverage has ended the flawless idol while arguing that heroism rests on deeds rather than perfection, and that the media age has its own visible heroes; coherent and persuasive.

sentences.text: In a world of cameras, leaks, and relentless reporting, no public figure can keep their flaws hidden for long, and the statement concludes that heroism itself has become impossible.
It claims that in this age of intensive media coverage, a society can no longer regard any living man or woman as a hero.
Media exposure has certainly changed how we admire, but the statement is wrong, because heroism depends on what a person does, not on whether the cameras ever catch them being ordinary.

sections.role: Body — Media has ended the flawless idol

sentences.text: It is true that intensive coverage makes the old kind of flawless hero impossible.
Where past heroes were known through statues and carefully managed stories, today's are filmed, recorded, and subjected to constant scrutiny until every weakness is on display.
A general's temper, a champion's private failures, a leader's hypocrisies now reach millions, and the polished image cannot survive the exposure.
The pedestal, in the age of the smartphone, has become very hard to stay on.
So the statement is right that the spotless idol of earlier eras can no longer exist.

sections.role: Body — But heroism was never about being spotless

sentences.text: However, this confuses the loss of the flawless image with the loss of heroism itself.
A hero is a person who does something brave, selfless, or great, not a person without faults, and no amount of coverage of those faults can undo a courageous act.
We do not stop honoring a firefighter who saved a family, or a doctor who served through a plague, because the media later reveals that they were difficult at home.
Heroism attaches to the deed, and deeds are not erased by the discovery that the person who performed them was, like everyone, imperfect.
If anything, knowing that heroes are flawed human beings who rose to a great moment makes their courage more admirable, because it shows such courage is within ordinary reach.
The cameras reveal that heroes are people; they do not reveal that there are no heroes.
Courage shown in a crisis is not cancelled by rudeness shown at the dinner table.
What media coverage destroys is the myth of perfection, not the reality of greatness.

sections.role: Body — The media age has its own heroes

sentences.text: Moreover, the same media that exposes flaws also reveals heroism that earlier ages would never have seen.
Cameras now broadcast the ordinary rescuer, the whistleblower, the aid worker, and the protester, turning unknown people into widely admired figures.
We admire them with full knowledge of their humanity, which is a more honest admiration than the worship of distant, airbrushed idols ever was.
Across the world, living people are still revered for real courage and real sacrifice, which would be impossible if the statement were true.
If anything, a hero we know to be human is one we can actually hope to emulate.
Intensive coverage has not abolished heroes; it has only made us admire them with our eyes open.
In conclusion, the age of media coverage has changed heroism, not ended it.
It has killed the illusion of the flawless idol, but heroism, which rests on great deeds rather than perfect lives, survives the exposure unharmed.
We can still call the living heroes; we have simply learned to honor real people instead of polished myths.
